confidence_note: DB title 'Beden Dili'. Baseline and cluster reading are core to Navarro's method (Mind Tools, Throughline summaries). The old text's quote ('Limbic system reacts to stress...') is not verified and not used. No invented scene.
facts: Navarro warns that reading body language is not memorizing a sign dictionary.
Crossed arms can mean the person is cold or just comfortable, not always defensive.
The key step is a baseline: how this person normally behaves when relaxed.
A signal matters when it differs from the baseline.
Look for clusters of signals, not a single one.
People show stress differently: one goes still, another speeds up.
It takes observation and patience, not speed.
scene_details: Crossed arms in a cold room
The same person relaxed, then different
tension: The same gesture means two different things on two different people.
opening_idea: Open on crossed arms in a cold room.

lessons.idea: Learn how someone looks when relaxed before reading anything into a change.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A teammate who is always quiet versus one who suddenly goes quiet.

reflect_final: Think of someone close to you. What does their relaxed self look like, and what changes when they are under strain?

use_cases.move: Wait before judging; watch them over a few conversations.
Say 'you seem quieter than usual, is that right?'

pocket_idea: Crossed arms prove nothing alone: learn how someone sits when relaxed, then watch for the change.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A gesture means nothing until you know how that person normally sits.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Navarro: crossed arms may mean cold. First learn a person's baseline, then read the changes, in clusters.
